scope: Complete original nefness branch: smooth semipositive nef-big compact surface, exact smooth-positive unweakened divisor pole, full-mass E1 solution, zero Lelong numbers and incompleteness of every dense Zariski open positive regular locus. The distinct flow-compatible branch remains open.

exact_task.problem:
Let Y be a connected compact Kahler manifold, theta a smooth closed real (1,1)-form with nef and big cohomology class, D a nonempty simple-normal-crossing divisor, sigma its canonical defining section and |sigma|^2 a smooth Hermitian squared norm. Let dV_Y be a globally smooth strictly positive volume form, so the prescribed density |sigma|^(-2)dV_Y is a genuinely nonintegrable divisor pole with a coefficient smooth and strictly positive across the divisor. Use dd^c=(i/(2 pi)) partial barpartial. Let rho be the unique full-mass finite-energy solution in E^1(Y,theta) of
<(theta+dd^c rho)^n>=exp(rho)|sigma|^(-2)dV_Y,
where the non-pluripolar measure and the right side are extended by zero on D. Finite energy is relative to a minimal theta-psh potential, and full mass means the total non-pluripolar mass equals vol({theta}). The solution has the same Lelong numbers as a minimal potential. For nef and big classes it is smooth and theta+dd^c rho is strictly positive on a dense Zariski open locus.
Question: does nefness and bigness by itself force the induced positive metric to be complete on some dense Zariski open subset where it is smooth and strictly positive? Prove such completeness, or give a counterexample with all the displayed data and exact smooth-positive pole coefficient. The unrestricted big-class assertion has a known counterexample in a non-nef class; it does not decide this nef branch. Likewise, integrable logarithmically weakened poles with coefficients tending to zero at D do not answer this question. A counterexample must prove incompleteness of every candidate dense Zariski open positive regular locus, rather than merely observe that a proper restriction of a complete manifold can be incomplete.
This is the nefness branch of the original broader completeness research direction. The separate geometric-smoothing compatibility branch additionally constrains the class, divisor, discrepancies, semipositive residual and volume by specific flow data and must remain explicitly unclosed unless those hypotheses are also verified. Relevant primary source: Di Nezza, Guedj and Lu, Geometric smoothing by the Kahler-Ricci flow, arXiv:2607.08325v1, Section 3.1, Theorem 3.4 and Question 3.5. No candidate construction or proof is supplied.
exact_task.completionCriteria: Resolve completeness under mere nefness and bigness for the exact divisorial exponential equation, by complete universal proof or a fully explicit compact nef-big counterexample. If constructing a counterexample, prove the metric/divisor/smooth-positive-volume data globally, solve the actual equation, establish full mass and E^1 finite energy, prove smooth strict positivity on the asserted regular locus, and exhibit finite intrinsic length leading to an unavoidable missing boundary for every dense Zariski open regular locus. Prove existence and all asymptotics of any auxiliary ODE solution rather than use numerically tuned or asserted solutions. Do not weaken the prescribed pole coefficient or silently change the energy class. Verify external premises at primary sources and reconstruct the full proof independently. This is a complete answer to the nefness branch; do not claim the distinct flow-compatible branch or the whole original catalogue solved.

notes.summary: Constructs a smooth strictly convex radial profile F on R with 0<F'<1, an explicit bounded blow-up-end model, and an exact cusp-end ODE. The cusp solution is obtained by quadrature, not shooting; its asymptotics and all cancellation identities needed for a smooth volume coefficient are proved.
notes.detailedSummary: There is a C-infinity function F with p=F' in (0,1) and p'>0. For t<=-2, F=B-3 log(1-c exp(t/2)), with c=1/100 and some B, so pp'=K exp(F+t), K=(9c^2/8)exp(-B)>0, and p'~(3c/4)exp(t/2). For t>=2, let H(p)=(1-p)^2(1+2p)/6 and define p by t=2+integral from 3/4 to p of q/H(q)dq. Then F=t+log H(p), pp'=exp(F-t), 1-p~2/t, p'~2/t^2, and F-t=-2 log t+log 2+o(1). A positive-derivative interpolation of p on [-2,2] gives the global profile, with B determined by integration. These exact endpoint identities permit a smooth strictly positive volume form on the blow-up of P^2 at the origin, despite the fractional-power potential at the exceptional divisor and the cusp at infinity.
notes.text:
RADIAL PROFILE LEMMA

All derivatives below are with respect to the real variable t. We construct F in C-infinity(R) with
  0<F'(t)<1,  F''(t)>0,
and with the following exact models.

1. Blow-up end. Fix c=1/100. For t near and below -2 set
  L(t)=-3 log(1-c exp(t/2)),
  p_L(t)=L'(t)=(3/2)q/(1-q),  q=c exp(t/2).
Then
  p_L'(t)=(3/4)q/(1-q)^2,
  p_L p_L'=(9c^2/8) exp(t)(1-c exp(t/2))^(-3).
Consequently, if F=B+L on this end, then the exact identity is
  F' F''=K exp(F+t),  K=(9c^2/8)exp(-B)>0.
Also, as t tends to minus infinity,
  F=B+3c exp(t/2)+O(exp(t)),
  F''~(3c/4)exp(t/2).
The denominators are positive on a neighborhood of (-infinity,-2]. In particular p_L(-2)<1/50, say.

2. Cusp end. For 0<p<1 put
  H(p)=integral from p to 1 of (1-q)q dq
      =1/6-p^2/2+p^3/3
      =(1-p)^2(1+2p)/6.
This is positive, and H'(p)=(p-1)p. Define
  T(p)=2+integral from 3/4 to p of q/H(q)dq.
It is smooth and strictly increasing. The integral tends to infinity as p tends to 1, because q/H(q)~2/(1-q)^2. Thus T has a smooth inverse p_R(t) on [2,infinity), extending smoothly to a neighborhood of t=2. It satisfies
  p_R(2)=3/4,  p_R'=H(p_R)/p_R>0,
  p_R(t) tends to 1.
Define
  F_R(t)=t+log H(p_R(t)).
Direct differentiation, using H'=(p-1)p, gives
  F_R'=1+(H'/H)(H/p)=p_R,
  F_R''=H(p_R)/p_R,
  F_R' F_R''=H(p_R)=exp(F_R-t).
This proves existence and the exact ODE identity on the entire cusp end without a tuning or shooting argument.

For the asymptotics set q(t)=1-p_R(t). Then q decreases to zero and
  (1/q)'=p_R'/q^2=(3-2q)/(6(1-q)) tends to 1/2.
Integration and division by t imply 1/(tq) tends to 1/2. Hence
  1-p_R~2/t,
  H(p_R)~2/t^2,
  F_R''~2/t^2,
  F_R-t=-2 log t+log 2+o(1).
These are all endpoint asymptotics needed below. Higher derivative control at the divisor is unnecessary because the volume coefficient will cancel exactly, not just asymptotically.

3. Interpolation. We describe a rigorous positive-derivative interpolation between p_L at -2 and p_R at 2. Write d=p_R(2)-p_L(-2)>0. Choose disjoint sufficiently short endpoint collars in [-2,2], and smooth cutoffs alpha_L, alpha_R supported in those collars, respectively equal to 1 on still shorter endpoint collars. They take values in [0,1]. The endpoint functions p_L and p_R are defined on these collars. Choose a small number eta>0 and initially set
  Q_0=alpha_L p_L'+alpha_R p_R'+eta(1-alpha_L-alpha_R).
This is strictly positive and agrees with the required endpoint derivatives near the endpoints. By first shortening the collars and then reducing eta, its integral can be made less than d. Choose a nonzero nonnegative smooth bump b compactly supported in (-2,2), and set
  Q=Q_0+C b,
  C=(d-integral Q_0)/(integral b)>0.
Then Q>0, its integral is exactly d, and it retains the endpoint germs. Define on [-2,2]
  p(t)=p_L(-2)+integral from -2 to t of Q(x)dx.
Because its endpoint values and all derivative germs match, it patches smoothly with p_L for t<=-2 and p_R for t>=2. It is strictly increasing and satisfies 0<p<1 everywhere.

Finally define F by F(2)=F_R(2) and F'=p. Then F=F_R for t>=2 and F=B+L for t<=-2, with B determined by the integration. All stated endpoint identities hold exactly. The interpolation introduces no restriction on B, and K is strictly positive for every resulting B.

This completes the profile construction and independently proves existence and the asymptotics of the only auxiliary ODE used in the counterexample.

correctness.report: The profile construction is established. Direct differentiation gives both exact endpoint identities, including K=(9c^2/8)e^{-B}. The quadrature defining T is strictly increasing and diverges at p=1, so its inverse exists on the entire asserted cusp end. The identity (1/(1-p))'→1/2 proves all stated cusp asymptotics. The positive interpolation Q has the required integral and endpoint germs; consequently p patches smoothly, remains strictly between 0 and 1, and integrates to the required F. Both summaries accurately describe this supporting lemma rather than claiming an independent global counterexample.

source.report: The correctness check identified no nonroutine external premise.

reconstruction.report: The profile construction is valid. The quadrature has positive derivative and divergent right endpoint, and its inverse gives the asserted exact ODE and asymptotics. The positive-derivative interpolation matches both endpoint germs while retaining 0<p<1 and p'>0. Anchoring F at t=2 determines B, and the stated K gives the exact left identity. The original claim, extracted statement, independent proof, and both summaries are consistent; no shooting assumption or unproved endpoint asymptotic is used.
reconstruction.statement:
There exist B∈R and F∈C∞(R) with the following properties. All derivatives are taken with respect to t∈R. Set c=1/100, p=F', and K=(9c²/8)e^(−B). Then K>0, 0<p(t)<1, and p'(t)>0 for every t∈R.

Define q_L(t)=c e^(t/2) and L(t)=−3 log(1−q_L(t)) wherever q_L(t)<1. For every t≤−2,
F(t)=B+L(t),
p(t)=p_L(t):=(3/2)q_L(t)/(1−q_L(t)),
p'(t)=(3/4)q_L(t)/(1−q_L(t))²,
p(t)p'(t)=K e^(F(t)+t).
The function L is smooth on a neighborhood of (−∞,−2], p_L(−2)<1/50, and
p_L(t)p_L'(t)=(9c²/8)e^t(1−c e^(t/2))^(−3).
As t→−∞,
F(t)=B+3c e^(t/2)+O(e^t),
p'(t)∼(3c/4)e^(t/2).

For 0<a<1 define
H(a)=∫_a^1(1−b)b db=1/6−a²/2+a³/3=(1−a)²(1+2a)/6
and
T(a)=2+∫_(3/4)^a b/H(b) db.
Then H(a)>0, H'(a)=(a−1)a, and T is smooth and strictly increasing. Moreover, b/H(b)∼2/(1−b)² as b→1, and T(a)→+∞ as a→1. The inverse p_R=T^(−1) is defined and smooth on [2,+∞), extends smoothly to a neighborhood of t=2, and satisfies
p_R(2)=3/4,
p_R'(t)=H(p_R(t))/p_R(t)>0,
p_R(t)→1 as t→+∞.
Define F_R(t)=t+log H(p_R(t)). Then, on [2,+∞),
F_R'(t)=p_R(t),
F_R''(t)=H(p_R(t))/p_R(t),
F_R'(t)F_R''(t)=e^(F_R(t)−t).

The global function F can be chosen with F(2)=F_R(2), F(t)=F_R(t) and p(t)=p_R(t) for every t≥2, while retaining the stated left-end model and strict inequalities on all of R. In particular, for t≥2,
p(t)p'(t)=e^(F(t)−t).
As t→+∞,
1−p(t)∼2/t,
H(p(t))∼2/t²,
p'(t)∼2/t²,
F(t)−t=−2 log t+log 2+o(1).
reconstruction.proof:
We construct the profile, including its interpolation, explicitly up to a freely chosen smooth bump.

First consider the right end. Direct calculation gives
H(a)=1/6−a²/2+a³/3=(1−a)²(1+2a)/6,
H'(a)=(a−1)a.
Thus H is positive on (0,1), and T'(a)=a/H(a)>0. Moreover,
a/H(a)∼2/(1−a)² as a→1.
Integration of this asymptotic gives T(a)∼2/(1−a), in particular T(a)→∞. Since T(3/4)=2, the inverse p_R exists on [2,∞). The inverse function theorem also extends it smoothly to an open interval containing 2. It satisfies
p_R'=H(p_R)/p_R>0,
p_R(2)=3/4,
lim_{t→∞}p_R(t)=1.
For F_R=t+log H(p_R), the chain rule gives
F_R'=1+(H'(p_R)/H(p_R))p_R'=1+H'(p_R)/p_R=p_R,
F_R''=H(p_R)/p_R,
and hence F_R'F_R''=H(p_R)=exp(F_R−t).
Writing y=1−p_R(t), the asymptotic for T implies y∼2/t. Consequently
H(p_R)∼y²/2∼2/t²,
p_R'∼2/t²,
F_R−t=−2 log t+log 2+o(1).
These are proved asymptotics of the inverse, not a shooting or numerical construction.

For the left end, put q_L=c exp(t/2), with c=1/100. This is less than 1 on a neighborhood of (−∞,−2]. Differentiating L=−3 log(1−q_L) gives
L'=(3/2)q_L/(1−q_L)=p_L,
L''=(3/4)q_L/(1−q_L)²=p_L',
p_Lp_L'=(9c²/8)exp(t)(1−c exp(t/2))^(−3).
Both p_L and p_L' are strictly positive. Since exp(−1)<1/2, q_L(−2)<1/200, and therefore p_L(−2)<(3/2)/199<1/50. Taylor expansion of −log(1−q_L) gives
L(t)=3c exp(t/2)+O(exp(t)),
p_L'(t)∼(3c/4)exp(t/2)
as t→−∞.

It remains to join the two ends without losing strict convexity. Set a_L=p_L(−2) and Δ=3/4−a_L>0. Choose small, disjoint endpoint neighborhoods in [−2,2], on which p_L' and the smooth extension of p_R' are defined. Take smooth cutoff functions χ_L,χ_R with disjoint supports in those neighborhoods, equal to 1 near the respective endpoints, and between 0 and 1. For ε>0 define
a_0(t)=χ_L(t)p_L'(t)+χ_R(t)p_R'(t)+ε(1−χ_L(t)−χ_R(t)).
This is strictly positive. By first taking the endpoint supports sufficiently short, and then taking ε sufficiently small, we obtain ∫_{−2}^2 a_0(t)dt<Δ. Choose a nonnegative smooth bump b supported away from the endpoint neighborhoods, with integral 1, and set
a(t)=a_0(t)+(Δ−∫_{−2}^2 a_0)b(t).
Then a>0, its integral is Δ, and it agrees with the prescribed endpoint derivatives near both endpoints.

On [−2,2] define p(t)=a_L+∫_{−2}^t a(x)dx. Extend it by p_L on the left and p_R on the right. The values and all derivatives match: near −2 this follows by integrating the common derivative from the common value, and near 2 by integrating backwards from p(2)=3/4=p_R(2). Thus p is smooth on R, p'>0 everywhere, and 0<p<1. On the joining interval it lies between a_L and 3/4.

Finally define
F(t)=F_R(2)+∫_2^t p(x)dx,
B=F_R(2)−∫_{−2}^2 p(x)dx−L(−2),
K=(9c²/8)exp(−B).
Then F is smooth, F'=p, F=F_R on [2,∞), and F=B+L on (−∞,−2]. In particular K>0, and on the left
pp'=(9c²/8)exp(t+L)=K exp(F+t).
On the right pp'=exp(F−t), as already proved. The stated left expansion for F follows by adding B to the expansion of L, and all right-end asymptotics follow from the inverse construction above. This proves every assertion of the note.

notes.summary: Complete counterexample for mere nefness and bigness: blow up P^2 at a point, take theta in the pullback hyperplane class and D the disjoint line at infinity. The explicit radial solution has an exact smooth-positive divisor-pole coefficient, full mass and E^1 energy, a cusp at D, and finite distance to every point of the nonsmooth exceptional divisor. Every dense Zariski open positive regular locus is incomplete. No flow-compatibility claim is made.
notes.detailedSummary: Let Y=Bl_P P^2, P=[1:0:0], E the exceptional curve, and D the inverse image of Z0=0. A smooth convex regularization U(t) of max(0,t), equal to 0 for t<=-1 and t for t>=1, defines a smooth semipositive Hermitian curvature theta in H=pi*O(1)=O(D), and |sigma|^2=exp(-U) on the affine chart. H is nef and big; an explicit Kähler-current decomposition follows from the incidence embedding Y into P^2 x P^1. Use the profile F of n1 and rho=F(log|z|^2)-U(log|z|^2), with rho=B on E and rho=-infinity on D. Put Omega=dd^c F on Y minus E union D and dV_Y=exp(-F)Omega^2 there. In exceptional coordinates z=(u,uv), h=1+|v|^2, the exact origin identity gives dV_Y=(2K/pi^2)h^(-1)dLambda. In infinity coordinates z=(1/w,v/w), the exact cusp identity gives dV_Y=(2/pi^2)h^(-3)dLambda. Hence dV_Y extends globally smooth and strictly positive, and the prescribed pole is exactly (2/pi^2)|w|^(-2)h^(-2)dLambda near D. The equation follows identically from |sigma|^2=exp(-U). The total non-pluripolar mass is integral 2F'F''dt=1=vol(H). Direct mixed-energy integrals and bounded truncation shell masses prove E^1 without a specialized existence theorem. Omega is smooth Kähler on Y minus E union D. Its normal coefficient at E behaves as a positive constant divided by |u|, so it is nonsmooth at every exceptional point but radial lengths to E are finite. For any dense Zariski open regular locus, a generic point of E avoids all other components of the analytic complement, yielding a finite-length curve inside that locus with an unavoidable missing endpoint. This negatively resolves precisely the nef-big branch; the separate flow-compatible branch is unverified.
notes.text:
A COMPLETE NEF-AND-BIG COUNTEREXAMPLE

We use dd^c=(i/(2 pi)) partial barpartial throughout. The profile F, constants c and B, and positive constant K are those constructed and proved in n1. Write p=F'. Thus 0<p<1 and p'=F''>0 everywhere, and
  pp'=K exp(F+t) for t<=-2,
  pp'=exp(F-t) for t>=2.
At the two ends,
  F=B+3c exp(t/2)+O(exp(t)),  p'~(3c/4)exp(t/2) as t tends to minus infinity,
  1-p~2/t,  p'~2/t^2,
  F-t=-2 log t+log 2+o(1) as t tends to infinity.

I. THE COMPACT MANIFOLD AND THE NEF-BIG CLASS

Let X=P^2 with homogeneous coordinates [Z0:Z1:Z2], let P=[1:0:0], and let pi:Y->X be its blow-up at P. For an explicit projective model,
  Y={([Z0:Z1:Z2],[ell1:ell2]) in P^2 x P^1 : Z1 ell2=Z2 ell1}.
This is the smooth incidence surface, and its embedding in the product makes it compact, connected, and Kähler. Let f:Y->P^1 be the second projection. Let E=pi^(-1)(P), and let
  D=pi^(-1)({Z0=0}).
D is a smooth nonempty divisor, isomorphic to P^1, disjoint from E. In particular it is simple normal crossing.

Write H=pi^*c1(O_P2(1)). It is nef, since it admits the smooth semipositive representative pi^*omega_FS; equivalently adding any positive multiple of a Kähler form gives a Kähler representative of the perturbed class. It is big by the following explicit current construction. If L=f^*c1(O_P1(1)), then L=H-[E]: the pullback of a line through P consists of its strict transform, a fiber of f, plus E. For epsilon>0 the form
  pi^*omega_FS+epsilon f^*omega_FS
is Kähler on Y, since (pi,f) is an embedding and this form is the restriction of a product Kähler form. Its class is H+epsilon L=(1+epsilon)H-epsilon[E]. Consequently
  (pi^*omega_FS+epsilon f^*omega_FS)/(1+epsilon)
       +(epsilon/(1+epsilon))[E]
is a Kähler current in H. Thus H is big. Also H^2=1, either by two generic lines missing P, or by the degree-one birational pullback computation.

II. A SMOOTH CURVATURE FORM AND THE EXACT HERMITIAN NORM

Choose an even, nonnegative, smooth function eta, positive on (-1,1), supported in [-1,1], with integral 1. Set
  U(t)=integral max(0,t-x) eta(x)dx.
Then U is smooth and convex,
  U=0 for t<=-1,  U=t for t>=1,
  U'>=0, U''>=0.
On the affine chart Z0!=0 put z=(Z1/Z0,Z2/Z0), s=|z|^2, and t=log s. Define a Hermitian metric on O_P2(1) by giving the frame Z0 squared norm exp(-U(t)). This is smooth at z=0 because U is identically zero there. At infinity, in the chart Z1!=0 write
  w=Z0/Z1,  v=Z2/Z1,  h=1+|v|^2.
Then s=h/|w|^2 and, near w=0, U=t, so the frame Z1 has squared norm
  exp(-U)/|w|^2=1/h.
This proves smoothness and strict positivity of the Hermitian metric across the line at infinity. The analogous chart with Z2!=0 covers its other points.

Pull this metric back to O_Y(D)=pi^*O_P2(1). Let sigma=pi^*Z0 be the canonical defining section of D, and let theta be its smooth Hermitian curvature. On the affine chart,
  |sigma|^2=exp(-U(t)),  theta=dd^c U(t).
On the infinity chart,
  |sigma|^2=|w|^2/h,  theta=dd^c log h.
The curvature is semipositive: away from the origin this follows from U'>=0 and U''>=0 in the radial Hessian, and near the origin it is zero. Thus theta is a globally smooth closed real (1,1)-form, semipositive, in the nef-big class H. It vanishes on a neighborhood of E. The constant potential 0 has minimal theta-psh singularities: any theta-psh function is bounded above on compact Y, and 0 itself is theta-psh. In particular the reference minimal potential can be taken to be 0, and the volume of the class is the mass of theta^2, namely 1.

III. THE POTENTIAL AND ITS POSITIVITY

On Y minus E union D, identified with C^2 minus {0}, define
  rho=F(t)-U(t),  Omega=theta+dd^c rho=dd^c F(t).
Extend rho to E by its limit B, and set rho=-infinity on D. It is globally upper semicontinuous and theta-psh, as we now check at the missing divisors.

The radial Hessian on C^2 minus {0} has eigenvalues p/s and p'/s; both are strictly positive. Hence Omega is smooth and strictly positive on
  U_0=Y minus (E union D),
a dense Zariski open subset.

Near E, use blow-up coordinates z1=u, z2=u v. Then s=|u|^2 h and t=log(|u|^2h). Since theta=0 there, the local potential is
  F(t)=B-3 log(1-c |u| sqrt(h)).
The function F(log|z|^2) on the base is psh off the origin and bounded above near it. Its upper semicontinuous extension is psh by the removable-singularity submean-value argument for locally bounded-above psh functions across an analytic set. Pulling back gives the stated continuous psh function near E. Thus there is no positivity problem at E.

Near D, theta has local potential log h, and rho+log h is psh off w=0 because its dd^c is Omega. It tends to minus infinity there, is locally bounded above, and therefore has the psh extension taking value minus infinity on w=0. Explicitly
  rho=F(t)-t=log H(p(t))=-2 log t+log 2+o(1),
where t=log(h/|w|^2). This proves positivity of the global current across D. The standard psh extension fact here can also be obtained directly by applying the submean inequality on transverse disks and taking an upper limit across w=0; local boundedness above is the necessary hypothesis.

All Lelong numbers of rho are zero. This is immediate from boundedness near E and smoothness elsewhere away from D. At D its growth is of log-log type, so rho/log|w| tends to zero. Thus rho has the same Lelong numbers as the minimal potential 0.

IV. THE GLOBALLY SMOOTH STRICTLY POSITIVE VOLUME FORM

On U_0 define
  dV_Y=exp(-F(t)) Omega^2.
We prove that this extends to a globally smooth strictly positive volume form, rather than merely one whose coefficient decays at D.

Let dLambda denote Euclidean Lebesgue volume in the indicated complex coordinates. The exact radial determinant formula in C^2 is
  Omega^2=(2/pi^2) pp'/s^2 dLambda_z.
The factor follows from our normalization dd^c=(i/(2pi)) partial barpartial.

At E, z=(u,uv), so dLambda_z=|u|^2 dLambda_(u,v) and s=|u|^2 h. Thus
  Omega^2=(2/pi^2) pp'/(|u|^2 h^2) dLambda_(u,v).
For all sufficiently small |u| the first exact endpoint identity gives pp'=K exp(F) s. Therefore
  dV_Y=(2K/pi^2) h^(-1) dLambda_(u,v).
This is smooth and strictly positive across u=0 and independent of u. The analogous exceptional chart covers the rest of E.

At D, z=(1/w,v/w), so dLambda_z=|w|^(-6)dLambda_(w,v), s=h/|w|^2, and
  Omega^2=(2/pi^2) pp'/(|w|^2 h^2) dLambda_(w,v).
For all sufficiently small |w|, the second exact endpoint identity gives exp(-F)pp'=exp(-t)=|w|^2/h. Hence
  dV_Y=(2/pi^2) h^(-3)dLambda_(w,v).
This is smooth and strictly positive across w=0. The chart with Z2!=0 gives the same conclusion at the other infinity points. These extensions agree on overlaps because they agree on the dense punctured overlaps, and smooth forms that agree there agree everywhere. On the intervening compact region dV_Y is already smooth and positive because F is smooth and Omega is Kähler. We have therefore constructed the required globally smooth strictly positive dV_Y.

In particular the prescribed pole is genuinely nonintegrable, with an exact smooth positive coefficient. Near D,
  |sigma|^(-2)dV_Y
      =(2/pi^2)|w|^(-2)h^(-2)dLambda_(w,v).
The coefficient (2/pi^2)h^(-2) is smooth and strictly positive at w=0, and the transverse integral of |w|^(-2) diverges logarithmically.

V. THE ACTUAL EQUATION AND FULL MASS

On U_0, since |sigma|^2=exp(-U),
  exp(rho)|sigma|^(-2)dV_Y
    =exp(F-U)exp(U)exp(-F)Omega^2
    =Omega^2.
This is the displayed equation with exactly the data just defined, not an asymptotic equation or a weakened logarithmic pole.

The non-pluripolar measure of the global current agrees with Omega^2 on U_0 and puts no mass on E or D. The right-hand side has no mass on E because it is absolutely continuous with respect to the smooth volume form there and rho is finite; it is extended by zero on D as required. Thus the equality on U_0 proves equality of the global measures.

For its mass, polar integration in C^2 gives
  integral Omega^2=integral from minus infinity to infinity of 2p(t)p'(t)dt
                  =p(infinity)^2-p(-infinity)^2
                  =1.
For completeness, dLambda_z has radial density pi^2 s ds; substitution in the determinant formula above gives exactly 2pp'dt after integrating the angular probability measure. Since the minimal-potential mass is integral theta^2=H^2=1, rho has full mass.

VI. FINITE ENERGY, CHECKED DIRECTLY

We give both the endpoint integrability estimates and a bounded-truncation energy argument, so that no specialized existence or finite-energy theorem is needed.

Near E, rho is bounded and theta=0. The only nonzero top-degree mixed measure relevant to the energy is Omega^2, whose density there is exp(F)(2K/pi^2)h^(-1), locally integrable. Hence all energy contributions near E are finite. On the compact region away from D and E everything is smooth and bounded.

Near D put
  alpha=dd^c t=dd^c log h,
  beta=(i/(2pi)) partial t wedge barpartial t.
Here alpha and beta have rank one, theta=alpha, and
  Omega=p alpha+p' beta,
  Omega^2=2pp' alpha wedge beta,
  Omega wedge theta=p' alpha wedge beta,
  theta^2=0.
Integration of alpha wedge beta over the angular and projective directions gives dt. Consequently the endpoint integrability reduces to
  integral_T^infinity |rho| p' dt<infinity,
  integral_T^infinity |rho| 2pp' dt<infinity,
which follow from |rho|=O(log t) and p'=O(t^(-2)).

To verify the E^1 definition by truncations, choose a constant M with phi=rho-M<=0, and set phi_k=max(phi,-k). For all large k, the truncation changes phi only sufficiently near D, since phi is bounded on the complement of any fixed neighborhood of D. On the cusp end phi=log H(p(t))-M is strictly decreasing to minus infinity. Let T_k be its unique crossing of -k. Thus
  k=2 log T_k+O(1).
Near D the local potential for theta+dd^c phi_k is
  G_k(t)=max(F(t)-M,t-k).
Its derivative equals p(t) before T_k and 1 after T_k, with an upward jump from p(T_k) to 1. Smooth convex regularization of this kink gives the radial mass formulas d((G_k')^2) for its square and d(G_k') for its wedge with theta. Therefore the kink contributes shell masses
  1-p(T_k)^2 to (theta+dd^c phi_k)^2,
  1-p(T_k) to (theta+dd^c phi_k) wedge theta.
Beyond the shell these top-degree mixed measures vanish because G_k is linear and theta has rank one. The potential is -k on the shell, so the absolute energy contributions from it are respectively
  k(1-p(T_k)^2),  k(1-p(T_k)),
both tending to zero, since 1-p(T_k)~2/T_k and k=O(log T_k). The formula for the shell square follows also by integrating 2q dq from p(T_k) to 1 during convex smoothing; it does not assume an ill-defined product of delta currents.

All interior energy integrals converge absolutely by the estimates already proved. Hence each of
  integral phi_k theta^2,
  integral phi_k (theta+dd^c phi_k) wedge theta,
  integral phi_k (theta+dd^c phi_k)^2
has a finite limit. In particular the usual relative Aubin-Mabuchi energies
  E_theta(phi_k)=(1/3) sum over j=0,1,2 of
     integral phi_k (theta+dd^c phi_k)^j wedge theta^(2-j)
are uniformly bounded below and have a finite limit. This is precisely finite E^1 energy relative to the minimal potential 0. Adding back M does not change finiteness. Thus rho belongs to E^1(Y,theta).

The bounded-potential wedge products used in this computation are the usual Bedford-Taylor products. Their radial formulas can be checked by the convex smoothings just described. At E the bounded psh extension has no mass on the analytic curve E (equivalently the radial boundary mass tends to zero because p(t) tends to zero). Thus there is no omitted boundary energy contribution. We have constructed the full-mass finite-energy solution itself; by the uniqueness stipulated in the question it is the solution denoted there by rho.

VII. FINITE DISTANCE TO AN UNAVOIDABLY MISSING EXCEPTIONAL DIVISOR

The form Omega is not smooth at any point of E. In the exceptional chart fix v=v_0 and put h_0=1+|v_0|^2. Its restriction to the transverse punctured disk is
  Omega|_(v=v_0)=(i/(2pi)) p'(log(|u|^2 h_0)) |u|^(-2) du wedge dbar u.
Since p'~(3c/4)exp(t/2), its normal coefficient is asymptotic to
  (3c sqrt(h_0)/4)|u|^(-1),
which diverges at every point u=0. Thus no point of E can belong to an open locus where the induced metric is smooth. Likewise at D the normal coefficient is asymptotic to 2/(|w|^2 t^2), which diverges, so D is not a smooth locus either. Consequently every dense Zariski open positive regular locus U is contained in U_0.

Nevertheless the radial approach to E has finite length. Along u=r>0, v=v_0, one has t=2 log r+log h_0. With the real Riemannian metric associated to Omega, the length is, up to the displayed fixed normalization,
  (1/(2 sqrt(pi))) integral from minus infinity to t_0 of sqrt(p'(t))dt.
This is finite because sqrt(p')=O(exp(t/4)) at the negative end. Equivalently the normal metric coefficient is of order 1/r, giving length integral of r^(-1/2)dr.

It remains essential to show incompleteness for every candidate dense Zariski open regular locus, rather than merely for U_0. Let U be any such locus, and let A=Y minus U be its proper closed analytic complement. Since E is wholly nonsmooth, E is contained in A. On the compact complex surface Y, the analytic set A has finitely many curve and point components. Any curve component other than E meets E in finitely many points; otherwise it would contain E as a component. Choose e in E avoiding those finite intersections and all point components. D is already disjoint from E. A sufficiently small coordinate neighborhood V of e therefore has
  A intersect V=E intersect V.
Choose exceptional coordinates (u,v) centered along that point, fix v=v_0, and take the radial curve u=r, 0<r<=r_0, entirely inside V. It lies in U and converges to e as r tends to zero. Its intrinsic metric length is finite by the preceding estimate. Points r_j tending to zero form a metric Cauchy sequence because the remaining tail lengths tend to zero. They have no limit in U: the smooth positive metric induces the ordinary manifold topology at every point of U, whereas their only limit in compact Y is the missing point e. Hence U is incomplete.

VIII. CONCLUSION AND SCOPE

These data satisfy every condition in the nef-and-big question: Y is compact connected Kähler; theta is globally smooth, closed, real and nef-big; D is nonempty smooth SNC; sigma has a smooth Hermitian squared norm; dV_Y is globally smooth and strictly positive; the prescribed density has an exact nonintegrable divisor pole with coefficient smooth and strictly positive across D; rho solves the actual exponential equation, is full mass and E^1, and has the minimal Lelong numbers; and its induced metric is smooth and strictly positive on U_0. Nevertheless every dense Zariski open positive regular locus is incomplete because of the unavoidable exceptional boundary.

Thus mere nefness and bigness do not force the asserted completeness. This is a complete negative resolution only of that branch. No specific geometric-smoothing flow data, discrepancy conditions, semipositive residual, or flow-prescribed volume have been verified here, so the separate flow-compatible branch remains explicitly unclosed.

reconstruction.statement:
Use dd^c=(i/(2π))∂∂̄. Let F,c,B,K and p=F' be the profile and constants of supporting note w7-1/n1. The following construction is a compact nef-and-big counterexample to completeness on every dense Zariski open positive regular locus.

Let X=P², with homogeneous coordinates [Z₀:Z₁:Z₂], let P=[1:0:0], and let π:Y→X be the blow-up of P. Equivalently,
Y={([Z₀:Z₁:Z₂],[ℓ₁:ℓ₂])∈P²×P¹: Z₁ℓ₂=Z₂ℓ₁}.
Let f:Y→P¹ be the second projection, E=π^(−1)(P), and D=π^(−1)({Z₀=0}). Then Y is a smooth connected compact Kähler surface, E is its exceptional curve, and D is a nonempty smooth divisor isomorphic to P¹ and disjoint from E; in particular, D is simple normal crossing. Write H=π* c₁(O_P²(1)). The class H is nef and big, and H²=1. Writing L=f* c₁(O_P¹(1)), one has L=H−[E]. For every ε>0, π*ω_FS+ε f*ω_FS is a Kähler form in the class (1+ε)H−ε[E], and
(π*ω_FS+ε f*ω_FS)/(1+ε)+(ε/(1+ε))[E]
is a Kähler current in H. Here the Fubini–Study forms represent the respective hyperplane classes, and [E] in the displayed current denotes integration over E.

Choose an even nonnegative η∈C∞(R), supported in [−1,1], positive on (−1,1), and satisfying ∫_R η(x)dx=1. Define
U(t)=∫_R max(0,t−x)η(x)dx.
Then U is smooth and convex, U(t)=0 for t≤−1, U(t)=t for t≥1, and U',U''≥0. On {Z₀≠0}, put z=(Z₁/Z₀,Z₂/Z₀), s=|z|², and t=log s. Give the local frame Z₀ of O_P²(1) squared norm e^(−U(t)), extended as 1 at z=0. This defines a globally smooth strictly positive Hermitian metric on O_P²(1). In the chart {Z₁≠0}, with
w=Z₀/Z₁, v=Z₂/Z₁, h=1+|v|²,
one has s=h/|w|², and near w=0 the frame Z₁ has squared norm 1/h. The analogous prescription holds in the chart {Z₂≠0}.

Pull this Hermitian metric back to O_Y(D)≅π*O_P²(1), let σ=π*Z₀ be the defining section of D, and let θ be the metric's curvature. Then θ is a globally smooth closed real semipositive (1,1)-form representing H. On the affine chart,
|σ|²=e^(−U(t)), θ=dd^c U(t).
Near D in the above infinity coordinates,
|σ|²=|w|²/h, θ=dd^c log h.
The form θ vanishes on a neighborhood of E. The potential 0 has minimal θ-plurisubharmonic singularities, all its Lelong numbers are zero, and
vol({θ})=∫_Y θ²=1.

Identify U₀:=Y\(E∪D) with C²\{0}. On U₀ define
ρ=F(t)−U(t), Ω=θ+dd^cρ=dd^c F(t).
Extend ρ by the value B on E and by −∞ on D. The resulting function is globally upper semicontinuous and θ-plurisubharmonic. It is continuous near E, smooth on U₀, and has zero Lelong number at every point of Y. The form Ω is smooth and strictly positive on the dense Zariski open subset U₀. On C²\{0}, the complex Hessian of F(log|z|²) has eigenvalues p/s and p'/s.

In exceptional coordinates z=(u,uv), put h=1+|v|², so t=log(|u|²h). For sufficiently small |u|,
θ=0, ρ=F(t)=B−3 log(1−c|u|√h).
Near D, with t=log(h/|w|²), one has
ρ=F(t)−t=log H(p(t))=−2 log t+log 2+o(1),
where H(a)=(1−a)²(1+2a)/6 is the function of w7-1/n1.

Initially define on U₀
 dV_Y=e^(−F(t))Ω².
This volume form extends to a globally smooth strictly positive volume form on Y. With dΛ denoting ordinary Euclidean Lebesgue volume in the indicated complex coordinates, its exact local formulas are as follows:
Ω²=(2/π²)(pp'/s²)dΛ_z;
in exceptional coordinates z=(u,uv),
Ω²=(2/π²)pp'/(|u|²h²)dΛ_(u,v),
and, for all sufficiently small |u|,
dV_Y=(2K/π²)h^(−1)dΛ_(u,v);
in infinity coordinates z=(1/w,v/w),
Ω²=(2/π²)pp'/(|w|²h²)dΛ_(w,v),
and, for all sufficiently small |w|,
dV_Y=(2/π²)h^(−3)dΛ_(w,v).
The analogous formulas hold in the other exceptional and infinity charts, and the smooth extensions agree on overlaps. Consequently, near D the prescribed density is exactly
|σ|^(−2)dV_Y=(2/π²)|w|^(−2)h^(−2)dΛ_(w,v).
Its coefficient (2/π²)h^(−2) is smooth and strictly positive across D, and the prescribed density is genuinely nonintegrable along D.

The global non-pluripolar equation is
⟨(θ+dd^cρ)²⟩=e^ρ|σ|^(−2)dV_Y,
with the right side extended by zero on D. On U₀ both sides equal Ω², and both measures assign zero mass to E∪D. The non-pluripolar mass is
∫_Y⟨(θ+dd^cρ)²⟩=∫_U₀ Ω²=∫_(−∞)^(+∞)2p(t)p'(t)dt=1=vol({θ}).
Thus ρ has full mass.

The potential ρ belongs to E¹(Y,θ) relative to the minimal potential 0. More precisely, the following energy conclusions hold. Near E, ρ is bounded, θ=0, and Ω² has locally integrable density e^F(2K/π²)h^(−1) in exceptional coordinates. Near D set
α=dd^c t=dd^c log h,
β=(i/(2π))∂t∧∂̄t.
There α and β have rank one, θ=α, and
Ω=pα+p'β,
Ω²=2pp'α∧β,
Ω∧θ=p'α∧β,
θ²=0.
Integration of α∧β over all angular and projective directions has radial density dt. For every sufficiently large T,
∫_T^∞ |ρ(t)|p'(t)dt<∞,
∫_T^∞ |ρ(t)|2p(t)p'(t)dt<∞,
where ρ(t)=F(t)−t on this end.

Choose M∈R with φ:=ρ−M≤0, and set φ_k=max(φ,−k). For every sufficiently large k, φ_k differs from φ only on the cusp end. There is a unique T_k≥2 satisfying
log H(p(T_k))−M=−k,
and T_k→∞ with k=2 log T_k+O(1). On the punctured cusp end,
θ+dd^cφ_k=dd^c G_k(t),
G_k(t)=max(F(t)−M,t−k).
The derivative of G_k equals p(t) for t<T_k and 1 for t>T_k, with one-sided jump from p(T_k) to 1. The bounded-potential measures (θ+dd^cφ_k)² and (θ+dd^cφ_k)∧θ have respective total shell masses on {t=T_k}
1−p(T_k)² and 1−p(T_k).
For t>T_k, θ+dd^cφ_k=θ and all the top-degree mixed measures above vanish. Since φ_k=−k on the shell, its absolute shell contributions to the two energy integrals are respectively
k(1−p(T_k)²) and k(1−p(T_k)),
and both tend to zero. There is no additional boundary mass on E. For j=0,1,2, each integral
∫_Y φ_k(θ+dd^cφ_k)^j∧θ^(2−j)
has a finite limit as k→∞. In particular, the bounded-potential Aubin–Mabuchi energies
E_θ(φ_k)=(1/3)∑_(j=0)^2∫_Y φ_k(θ+dd^cφ_k)^j∧θ^(2−j)
are uniformly bounded below and have a finite limit. These conclusions use the bounded-potential Bedford–Taylor products. The constructed ρ is therefore the full-mass finite-energy solution specified in the task and has the same Lelong numbers as a minimal potential.

Neither E nor D contains a point at which Ω is smooth. In the exceptional chart, for fixed v=v₀ and h₀=1+|v₀|²,
Ω|_(v=v₀)=(i/(2π))p'(log(|u|²h₀))|u|^(−2)du∧dū,
and its coefficient inside i/(2π) is asymptotic to
(3c√h₀/4)|u|^(−1)
as u→0. Near D, on a fixed-v transverse disk, the corresponding coefficient is p'(t)/|w|²∼2/(|w|²t²), and also diverges.

For the real Riemannian metric g(X,Y)=Ω(X,JY) on U₀, the radial path u=r>0, v=v₀, with t=2 log r+log h₀, has length from E to a point with parameter t₀ equal to
(1/(2√π))∫_(−∞)^t₀ √p'(t)dt<∞.
Moreover, for every dense Zariski open subset U⊂Y on which Ω is smooth and strictly positive, U⊂U₀, and there exist e∈E and a coordinate neighborhood V of e such that
(Y\U)∩V=E∩V.
In exceptional coordinates in V there is a radial curve u=r, v=v₀, 0<r≤r₀, lying entirely in U, having finite intrinsic g-length, and converging in Y to e as r→0. Points on this curve tending to e form a metric Cauchy sequence with no limit in U. Consequently every dense Zariski open positive regular locus is incomplete.

This counterexample resolves negatively only the branch imposing mere nefness and bigness. It asserts no compatibility with the separate geometric-smoothing flow hypotheses, discrepancy conditions, semipositive residual, or flow-prescribed volume; that branch remains unclosed here.
reconstruction.proof:
We use the profile established in w7-1/n1 and the external premises expressly permitted in this note. All subsequent geometric, analytic, and metric computations are given below.

1. The compact surface and the nef-and-big class.

The incidence surface in the statement is the blow-up of P=[1:0:0] in P². Near P its two standard charts have blow-down coordinates z=(u,uv) and z=(u'v',u'); away from the exceptional curve the blow-down is an isomorphism. These charts establish smoothness, and E is a copy of P¹. The incidence surface is a connected compact complex submanifold of P²×P¹. The restriction of the product Kähler form shows that it is Kähler. The line {Z₀=0} avoids P, so its inverse image D is a smooth copy of P¹ disjoint from E. In particular D is nonempty and simple normal crossing.

Write H=π*c₁(O_{P²}(1)) and L=f*c₁(O_{P¹}(1)). A line through P has total transform equal to E plus the corresponding fiber of f, each with multiplicity one; hence H=[E]+L. Also H²=1: this follows, for example, by integrating the pullback of the Fubini–Study square, since π is an isomorphism off sets of measure zero and the hyperplane class on P² has square 1.

The form π*ω_FS is semipositive, so H is nef. For every ε>0 the form π*ω_FS+ε f*ω_FS is Kähler: it is the restriction to the incidence surface of a Kähler form on the product. Its class is H+εL=(1+ε)H−ε[E]. It follows that
(π*ω_FS+ε f*ω_FS)/(1+ε)+(ε/(1+ε))[E]
is a closed positive current in H dominating a Kähler form. Thus H is big. This verifies both nefness and bigness without assuming either from the desired conclusion.

2. The globally smooth divisor metric and θ.

An admissible η exists by normalizing the even bump exp(−1/(1−x²)) for |x|<1, extended by zero. For any η as in the statement,
U'(t)=∫_{−∞}^t η(x)dx,
U''(t)=η(t).
Thus U is smooth and convex. It vanishes for t≤−1. For t≥1, evenness gives ∫xη(x)dx=0, and consequently U(t)=t. In particular U',U''≥0.

On {Z₀≠0}, assign the frame Z₀ squared norm exp(−U(log|z|²)). This is smooth at z=0 because it equals 1 in a neighborhood of zero. In the chart Z₁≠0, put w=Z₀/Z₁, v=Z₂/Z₁, h=1+|v|². There t=log(h/|w|²), and the change of frame Z₁=Z₀/w gives
|Z₁|²=|w|^(−2)exp(−U(t)).
For sufficiently small |w| this equals 1/h. It therefore extends smoothly and strictly positively over w=0. The same calculation applies in the Z₂ chart. The transition identities already hold off the infinity line, and hence hold on it as well. We have obtained a globally smooth positive Hermitian metric on O_{P²}(1).

Its curvature is semipositive. Indeed, on the affine punctured chart the Hessian of U(log|z|²) has eigenvalues U'/|z|² and U''/|z|²; near zero it is zero, and near infinity its potential in the Z₁ frame is log h. Pulling the metric back to O_Y(D)=π*O_{P²}(1), and setting σ=π*Z₀, gives the smooth semipositive curvature form θ in H. The formulas are
|σ|²=exp(−U(t)), θ=dd^cU(t)
on the affine chart, and
|σ|²=|w|²/h, θ=dd^c log h
near D. Because U vanishes near z=0, θ vanishes in a neighborhood of E.

Since θ≥0, the potential 0 is θ-psh. Every θ-psh potential on compact Y is bounded above, so 0 has minimal singularities. Its Lelong numbers are zero. The permitted volume premise applies because θ is smooth, closed, semipositive and its class has just been proved big. Therefore vol({θ})=∫_Y θ²=H²=1.

3. The global potential, positivity, and Lelong numbers.

Identify U₀=Y\(E∪D) with C²\{0}. Define ρ=F(t)−U(t), t=log|z|². Then
Ω=θ+dd^cρ=dd^cF(t).
For s=|z|², the Hessian matrix of F(log s) is
(p/s)I+((p'−p)/s²)(bar z_j z_k)_{j,k}.
Its eigenvalues are p/s and p'/s. Both are positive by w7-1/n1. Thus Ω is smooth and strictly positive on U₀.

Near E use z=(u,uv), h=1+|v|², t=log(|u|²h). For sufficiently small |u| the left profile and U=0 give exactly
ρ=B−3 log(1−c|u|√h), θ=0.
This tends to B continuously. Its local potential is psh off E and locally bounded above near E. Applying the permitted psh-extension premise extends it psh across E with value B.

Near D, U=t and the right profile gives exactly
ρ=F(t)−t=log H(p(t)), t=log(h/|w|²).
In particular
ρ=−2 log t+log 2+o(1).
Here θ=dd^c log h, so a local potential for the total current is ρ+log h. It is psh off D, bounded above near D, and tends to −∞ uniformly as w→0 in a relatively compact v chart. The same extension premise extends it psh, with value −∞ on D. These local constructions agree with ρ on U₀, establishing a globally upper semicontinuous θ-psh potential with the stated values and regularity.

Its Lelong numbers vanish. This is immediate on U₀ and near E, where the local potentials are respectively smooth and bounded. At a point of D, on a fixed-v transverse disk the local potential has size −2 log(−log|w|²)+O(1). Its supremum on a small coordinate ball is bounded above and is bounded below by its value at a transverse point with |w| comparable to the radius. Dividing by log of the radius gives limit zero, which is the Lelong-number characterization by these suprema. Thus it also has zero Lelong number on D, agreeing everywhere with a minimal potential.

4. Exact volume-form computation and the unweakened pole.

Let dΛ denote ordinary Euclidean Lebesgue measure in the indicated two complex variables. With dd^c=i∂∂bar/(2π), the Hessian determinant above yields
Ω²=(2/π²)(pp'/s²)dΛ_z.
The complex Jacobian of z=(u,uv) is u. Since s=|u|²h, this becomes
Ω²=(2/π²)pp'/(|u|²h²)dΛ_(u,v).
The complex Jacobian of z=(1/w,v/w) is −1/w³. Since s=h/|w|², the infinity formula is
Ω²=(2/π²)pp'/(|w|²h²)dΛ_(w,v).

On U₀ define dV_Y=exp(−F(t))Ω². This is a smooth strictly positive volume form there. At the left end the exact ODE identity pp'=K exp(F+t) gives
exp(−F)Ω²=(2K/π²)h^(−1)dΛ_(u,v).
This is smooth and strictly positive across u=0. At the right end pp'=exp(F−t) gives
exp(−F)Ω²=(2/π²)h^(−3)dΛ_(w,v),
which is smooth and strictly positive across w=0. The corresponding formulas in the other exceptional and infinity charts give the same forms: they agree on the dense overlaps inside U₀, so their smooth extensions agree everywhere on the overlaps. Hence dV_Y is globally smooth and strictly positive on Y.

Combining the infinity formula with |σ|²=|w|²/h gives the exact expression
|σ|^(−2)dV_Y=(2/π²)|w|^(−2)h^(−2)dΛ_(w,v).
The coefficient is smooth and strictly positive at every point of D. Integrating in a transverse w disk contains a positive multiple of ∫₀^δ dr/r, so this prescribed density really is nonintegrable. No coefficient tending to zero, or logarithmically weakened pole, has been used.

5. The equation and full mass.

On U₀,
exp(ρ)|σ|^(−2)dV_Y
=exp(F−U)exp(U)exp(−F)Ω²=Ω².
The non-pluripolar measure agrees with this ordinary wedge there and assigns zero mass to E∪D by the permitted premise. The right side, extended by zero on D as required, likewise gives no mass to E or D: away from D it is a density with respect to a smooth volume form, and E has volume zero. Thus the displayed equation holds globally as an equality of measures.

For a radial integrand, Euclidean polar coordinates in C² give dΛ_z radial density π²s ds=π²exp(2t)dt. Consequently
∫_Y⟨(θ+dd^cρ)²⟩=∫_{−∞}^∞2p(t)p'(t)dt
=[p(t)²]_{−∞}^{∞}=1.
The endpoint values are 0 and 1 by w7-1/n1. This equals vol({θ}), so ρ has full mass.

6. Finite energy, including the truncation shells.

Here we verify the bounded-potential energy criterion from the permitted premises, rather than inferring finite energy solely from full mass.

On U₀ put
α=dd^c t, β=(i/(2π))∂t∧∂bar t, a=U'.
Both α and β have rank one, and α²=β²=0. The formulas are
θ=aα+a'β, Ω=pα+p'β,
θ²=2aa'α∧β,
Ω∧θ=(ap'+pa')α∧β,
Ω²=2pp'α∧β.
Comparison with the volume formula proves α∧β=(1/(π²s²))dΛ_z. Thus integration over all angular and projective directions gives exactly radial density dt for α∧β.

In particular, near D, a=1 and a'=0, so θ=α and
Ω∧θ=p'α∧β, Ω²=2pp'α∧β, θ²=0.
The right-end asymptotics give |ρ(t)|=O(log t) and p'(t)=O(t^(−2)). Hence both
∫_T^∞|ρ(t)|p'(t)dt and ∫_T^∞|ρ(t)|2p(t)p'(t)dt
are finite. Near E, ρ is bounded and θ=0. The exact volume formula there reads Ω²=exp(F)(2K/π²)h^(−1)dΛ_(u,v), a locally integrable density. Since the local potential is bounded there, the permitted Bedford–Taylor premise also rules out any additional mass on E.

The potential is bounded above globally. Choose M with φ=ρ−M≤0 and put φ_k=max(φ,−k). The closure of {t≤2}, including E, is compact and φ is continuous there. For all sufficiently large k no truncation occurs on that set. On t≥2,
φ(t)=log H(p(t))−M,
whose derivative is p−1<0 and whose limit is −∞. There is therefore a unique T_k≥2 with
log H(p(T_k))−M=−k.
It tends to infinity, and the established right asymptotic gives k=2 log T_k+O(1).

On the punctured cusp,
θ+dd^cφ_k=dd^cG_k(t),
G_k(t)=max(F(t)−M,t−k).
For t<T_k its derivative is p(t); for t>T_k its derivative is 1. At T_k the derivative jumps from p(T_k) to 1.

For clarity, the resulting shell masses can be obtained within the permitted Bedford–Taylor framework. Smooth the convex function G_k by convolution in t near its corner. The resulting smooth convex radial potentials converge locally uniformly to G_k and are psh, since their first derivatives are positive and their second derivatives are nonnegative. Their top-degree radial measure is d((G_k')²), and their mixed measure with α has radial measure d(G_k'). Local uniform Bedford–Taylor convergence then gives the corresponding distributional derivatives at the corner. Thus the total shell masses are respectively
1−p(T_k)² for (θ+dd^cφ_k)²,
1−p(T_k) for (θ+dd^cφ_k)∧θ.
For t>T_k, φ_k=−k and θ+dd^cφ_k=θ, so all relevant top-degree measures vanish there, including near D. There is no additional mass on D, since φ_k is constant in a neighborhood of it, and none on E, by the bounded-potential no-pluripolar-mass premise.

We can consequently write the three energy integrals exactly, for sufficiently large k:
I_{0,k}=∫_Y φ_kθ²=∫_{−∞}^{∞}φ(t)2a(t)a'(t)dt,
I_{1,k}=∫_Y φ_k(θ+dd^cφ_k)∧θ
=∫_{−∞}^{T_k}φ(t)(a(t)p'(t)+p(t)a'(t))dt−k(1−p(T_k)),
I_{2,k}=∫_Y φ_k(θ+dd^cφ_k)²
=∫_{−∞}^{T_k}φ(t)2p(t)p'(t)dt−k(1−p(T_k)²).
Here φ(t)=F(t)−U(t)−M. The first integrand is supported in [−1,1]. In the second, its non-cusp portion has compact t support because a=a'=0 on the left. In the third, φ is bounded at the left end and pp'=O(exp(t)), so its left tail is integrable. Their right tails are integrable by the log(t)/t² estimates above.

Finally 1−p(T_k)∼2/T_k, while k=O(log T_k). Therefore both shell terms tend to zero. Each I_{j,k} has a finite limit. In particular
E_θ(φ_k)=(I_{0,k}+I_{1,k}+I_{2,k})/3
is uniformly bounded below and has a finite limit. The finitely many smaller truncations have finite energies because they are bounded θ-psh potentials.

All hypotheses of the permitted energy criterion now hold: θ is smooth semipositive with big class, 0 is the minimal reference, φ≤0 is θ-psh, and it has full non-pluripolar mass. Hence φ∈E¹(Y,θ), and invariance under adding constants gives ρ∈E¹(Y,θ). Together with the equation, this identifies ρ with the unique solution specified in the task. It also establishes every stated energy assertion using bounded-potential Bedford–Taylor products.

7. The singular curves cannot belong to a positive smooth regular locus.

Fix v=v₀ in an exceptional chart and put h₀=1+|v₀|². Restricting Ω to this transverse disk gives
Ω|_{v=v₀}=(i/(2π))p'(log(|u|²h₀))|u|^(−2)du∧dbar u.
The left asymptotic shows that its coefficient inside i/(2π) is
p'(log(|u|²h₀))/|u|²∼(3c√h₀/4)|u|^(−1).
It diverges at u=0. A smooth form in a neighborhood of any point of E would have bounded coefficients on this disk, so Ω cannot be smooth at any point of E. The other exceptional chart covers the remaining points.

Likewise, on a fixed-v transverse disk near D the coefficient is p'(t)/|w|². It is asymptotic to 2/(|w|²t²), which diverges as w→0. Thus no point of D is a point of smoothness either. Every open set on which the induced current is a smooth positive metric must therefore be contained in U₀.

8. Finite distance to an unavoidable boundary in every dense Zariski open regular locus.

For the Riemannian metric g(X,Y)=Ω(X,JY), the exceptional transverse disk has radial metric coefficient p'(t)/(πr²), where u=r>0 and t=2 log r+log h₀. The length of its radial curve from r=0 to a point with parameter t₀ is consequently
(1/√π)∫₀^{r₀}√p'(2 log r+log h₀) dr/r
=(1/(2√π))∫_{−∞}^{t₀}√p'(t)dt.
This is finite, since √p'(t) is asymptotic to √(3c/4)exp(t/4) at the left end.

Let U be any dense Zariski open subset of Y on which Ω is smooth and strictly positive. By the previous section U⊂U₀. Its complement A is a proper closed analytic subset containing E. The expressly permitted analytic-subset premise on compact surfaces therefore supplies a point e∈E and a neighborhood V with A∩V=E∩V. Choose exceptional coordinates in V, with e=(0,v₀), and take r₀ sufficiently small. The entire punctured radial curve u=r, v=v₀, 0<r≤r₀, then lies in U. It has the finite intrinsic length calculated above and converges in Y to e.

Points on this curve with r→0 form a Cauchy sequence for the intrinsic metric on its component of U: their mutual distances are bounded by the corresponding tail lengths, which tend to zero. They cannot have an intrinsic-metric limit in U. Indeed a smooth positive Riemannian metric induces the manifold topology locally (a positive lower bound for the metric on a relatively compact coordinate ball bounds the length needed to leave that ball). Any intrinsic-metric limit would thus also be their limit in Y. That limit is e, which does not belong to U. Hence U is incomplete.

This argument applies to every candidate dense Zariski open positive regular locus; it is not the observation that an arbitrary proper restriction of a complete metric may be incomplete. It proves the claimed compact nef-big counterexample with an exact smooth-positive divisorial pole coefficient. Only the mere-nefness-and-bigness branch is resolved negatively. No verification of the additional geometric-smoothing flow data, discrepancies, semipositive residual, or prescribed flow volume has been made, so the separate flow-compatible branch remains unclosed.
